procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated November 24, 1965 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Revision Application No. 232 of 1965.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant challenged the order of the Special Judge before the High Court of Bombay in Criminal Revision Application No. 232 of 1965. The High Court confirmed the order of the Special Judge, holding that the assessment order was 'property' and 'valuable security' under s. 30 IPC, and that the allegations prima facie disclosed an offence under s. 420 IPC. Certain other objections raised before the High Court were also negatived.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's decision. The appellant's argument is that the assessment order is not 'property' or 'valuable security', and therefore the charge under s. 420 IPC is not satisfied. The State supports the High Court's view.

issue.issue_text: Whether an income-tax assessment order constitutes 'property' within the meaning of Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: The appellant was charged with conspiring to cheat income-tax authorities to obtain a favorable income-tax assessment.
A charge was framed under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The appellant objected, arguing that an income-tax assessment order is not 'property' as required by Section 420 IPC.
law: The Supreme Court interpreted the word 'property' as it appears in Section 420 of the IPC.
The Court held that 'property' does not necessarily need to have a monetary or market value in the hands of the person who is being cheated (the deliverer).
It is sufficient if the item, even if valueless to the deliverer, becomes a thing of value in the hands of the person who receives it as a result of the cheating.
application: The Court applied this legal principle to the income-tax assessment order.
It reasoned that even if the assessment order is not considered 'property' in the hands of the Income-tax Officer, it becomes 'property' once it is in the hands of the assessee.
This is because the order is of great importance to the assessee, as it contains the official computation of their assessable income and determines their tax liability.
By obtaining a favorable assessment order through cheating, the assessee receives a document of significant value to them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument and held that an income-tax assessment order is 'property' within the meaning of Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code because it is a thing of value in the hands of the assessee who receives it.

issue.issue_text: Whether an income-tax assessment order can be considered a 'valuable security' for the purpose of framing a charge under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: The appellant was charged, among other offenses, under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for allegedly conspiring to cheat income-tax authorities, resulting in an incorrect assessment of a firm's income.
The appellant objected to the charge, arguing that an income-tax assessment order is not a 'property' and, specifically, not a 'valuable security' as required by Section 420.
The Special Judge and the High Court rejected these arguments, holding that an assessment order was indeed a 'valuable security'.
The appellant then appealed this decision to the Supreme Court.
law: Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) criminalizes cheating and dishonestly inducing the delivery of property or the making of a 'valuable security'.
Section 30 of the IPC defines a 'valuable security' as a document which purports to be a document whereby any legal right is created, extended, transferred, restricted, extinguished or released.

The Indian Income-tax Act's charging section (s. 3) is the provision that creates the liability to pay income tax. This liability arises upon the accrual of income, not upon the creation of an assessment order.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed whether an assessment order creates a 'legal right' and thus qualifies as a 'valuable security'.
The Court rejected the view of the lower courts, which had held that the order creates a right for the assessee to pay only the assessed amount and restricts their liability to that extent.

The Supreme Court's reasoning was that the legal liability to pay income tax is not created by the assessment order. Instead, this liability is created by the charging section of the Income-tax Act itself, and it arises at the point when the income accrues.
The assessment order is merely a procedural document that computes or quantifies this pre-existing liability; it does not create a new right or liability.
Since the assessment order does not create any legal right, it cannot be considered a 'valuable security' in the sense required by the IPC.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that an income-tax assessment order can, in no sense, be considered a 'valuable security' because it does not create any legal right; it only quantifies a pre-existing liability established by the Income-tax Act. Therefore, inducing an officer to make such an order does not satisfy the element of 'making a valuable security' required for a charge under Section 420 of the IPC.

issue.issue_text: Whether the framing of a charge under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code was correct in the circumstances of the case.

facts: The appellant was charged, along with others, with conspiracy to cheat income-tax authorities, leading to a charge under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
The charge alleged that the appellant dishonestly induced income-tax authorities to issue an assessment order for a lower amount of tax than was actually due.

The appellant challenged the framing of this charge, arguing that an assessment order is not 'property' or a 'valuable security' and that its issuance was not a 'delivery' as required by Section 420 IPC.
law: Section 420 of the IPC pertains to cheating and dishonestly inducing the delivery of any property or the making of a valuable security.
The appellant contended that the essential ingredients of this section were not met in this case.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the decisions of the lower courts (the Special Judge and the High Court), which had both rejected the appellant's arguments.
The High Court had specifically held that an income-tax assessment order is both 'property' and a 'valuable security' under Section 30 of the IPC.
The High Court also found that the allegations in the charge sheet did, prima facie, disclose an offence under Section 420.

The Supreme Court noted that its role at this preliminary stage was not to determine if the prosecution could ultimately prove its case, but only to decide whether a charge under Section 420 could be framed based on the circumstances.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court, agreeing with the reasoning of the lower courts, held that the framing of the charge under Section 420 IPC was correct in the circumstances of the case. Consequently, the Court rejected the appellant's challenge and dismissed the appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an income-tax assessment order constitutes 'property' within the meaning of Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: An income-tax assessment order is not 'property' and therefore the terms of Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code are not satisfied.
respondent_arguments: An income-tax assessment order is 'property', supporting the view expressed by the High Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an income-tax assessment order can be considered a 'valuable security' for the purpose of framing a charge under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: An income-tax assessment order is not a 'valuable security'.
respondent_arguments: An income-tax assessment order is a 'valuable security', supporting the view expressed by the High Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the framing of a charge under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code was correct in the circumstances of the case.
appellant_arguments: The framing of the charge under Section 420 was incorrect because the essential elements of the offence were not met, as an assessment order is neither 'property' nor a 'valuable security'.
respondent_arguments: The framing of the charge was correct as the allegations prima facie disclose an offence under Section 420, supporting the view of the High Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The word 'property' under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code does not necessarily mean that the thing delivered must have a monetary or market value in the hands of the person cheated. An item qualifies as 'property' if it is of significant importance to the recipient, such as an income-tax assessment order that determines tax liability.
obiter: As to whether the prosecution is able to make out its case, or not, is a different point.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court concluded that the framing of a charge under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code was correct. The Court's reasoning was not based on an independent analysis of whether an assessment order is 'property' or a 'valuable security', but rather on an affirmation of the lower courts' findings. It held that at the preliminary stage of framing a charge, the allegations that the accused fraudulently induced the income-tax authorities to issue an assessment order for a lesser amount were sufficient to prima facie constitute the offence, leaving the ultimate question of proof for the trial.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the allegations contained in a charge prima facie disclose the essential ingredients of an offence under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code for the purpose of framing the charge.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that an income-tax assessment order is neither 'property' nor a 'valuable security' was rejected at the charge-framing stage, as the Court accepted the High Court's contrary view for the purpose of allowing the trial to proceed.
